# Convex facet strips control relative missing-cap errors

This note proves a uniform interior-strip estimate for nonnegative
convex functions and transfers it to the missing radial volume
between a convex body and an enclosing simplex. No bound on the
ratio of the supremum to the integral is used. The conclusion is a
local cap-loss comparison, not a global stability theorem.

## 1. An explicit convex-function strip bound

Let \(F\) be a \(k\)-dimensional simplex, \(k\ge1\), with
normalized uniform probability \(\mu\), and let \(s_i\) be one
barycentric coordinate. Fix \(0<b<1\), and put
\[
r_{k,b}=\frac14\min\left\{b,\frac{1-b}{k}\right\},\qquad
C_{k,b}=\frac2{r_{k,b}}
=8\max\left\{\frac1b,\frac{k}{1-b}\right\}.
\tag{1}
\]
For every continuous nonnegative convex \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) and
every \(0\le\eta\le r_{k,b}\),
\[
\int_{\{|s_i-b|\le\eta\}} f\,d\mu
\le C_{k,b}\eta\int_F f\,d\mu .
\tag{2}
\]
The same constants apply to any affinely equivalent simplex.

Here is a direct proof. Given \(s_i=t\), the other barycentrics
are \((1-t)W\), where \(W\) is uniform on the opposite
\((k-1)\)-simplex. Define
\[
A(t)=\mathbb E_W f(t,(1-t)W),\qquad
M=\int_F f\,d\mu
=\int_0^1 k(1-t)^{k-1}A(t)\,dt.
\tag{3}
\]
For each fixed \(W\), the argument of \(f\) is affine in \(t\).
Therefore \(A\) is continuous, convex, and nonnegative. When
\(k=1\), \(W\) is a point and the same statements and formulas
hold, with marginal density one.

Write \(r=r_{k,b}\). If \(|t-b|\le\eta\le r\), then
\([t-r,t+r]\subset(0,1)\). Jensen at the midpoint gives
\[
A(t)\le\frac1{2r}\int_{t-r}^{t+r}A(s)\,ds
\le\frac{M}{2r\,k(1-t-r)^{k-1}}.
\tag{4}
\]
The second inequality uses nonnegativity and the minimum of the
beta density on that interval. Moreover \(1-t\ge(1-b)/2\) and
\(r\le(1-b)/(4k)\), so \(r/(1-t)\le1/(2k)\). Bernoulli's
inequality yields
\[
\left(1-\frac r{1-t}\right)^{k-1}
\ge1-\frac{k-1}{2k}\ge\frac12.
\]
Multiplying (4) by \(k(1-t)^{k-1}\) consequently gives
\[
k(1-t)^{k-1}A(t)\le M/r.
\tag{5}
\]
Integrating over the interval of length \(2\eta\) proves (2).
The argument remains valid when \(M=0\), and uses no endpoint
slope, Hessian, or supremum bound for \(f\).

## 2. Facet gauges and exact radial missing volume

Let \(S\) be a full \(d\)-dimensional simplex, \(d\ge2\), with
centroid \(g\), and let \(K\) be convex with
\[
g+(1-\delta)(S-g)\subseteq K\subseteq S,\qquad
0\le\delta<1.
\tag{6}
\]
Define the gauge of \(K\) about \(g\) by
\[
\rho(x)=\inf\{a>0:x-g\in a(K-g)\}.
\]
The inner inclusion makes this a finite continuous convex
function of \(x\). For every facet \(F\) of \(S\),
\[
1\le\rho(p)\le(1-\delta)^{-1}\quad(p\in F).
\]
Thus
\[
f_F(p)=\rho(p)-1
\tag{7}
\]
is continuous, nonnegative, and convex on \(F\).
If its facet centroid \(c_F\) belongs to \(K\), then
\(f_F(c_F)=0\). This additional zero is valid but is not needed
for the estimates in this note.

On the ray \(g+a(p-g)\), the missing part \(S\setminus K\)
has \(1/\rho(p)<a\le1\), up to null boundary conventions.
Its radial volume weight is exactly
\[
w_F(p)=1-\rho(p)^{-d}.
\tag{8}
\]
The elementary factorization
\[
\frac{1-\rho^{-d}}{\rho-1}
=\sum_{j=1}^d\rho^{-j}
\]
(interpreted by continuity at \(\rho=1\)) proves the uniform
comparison
\[
d(1-\delta)^d f_F\le w_F\le d f_F.
\tag{9}
\]

More precisely, if \(h_F=\operatorname{dist}(g,\operatorname{aff}F)\)
and \(d\sigma_F\) is Euclidean facet area, the cone Jacobian is
\(h_F a^{d-1}\,da\,d\sigma_F(p)\). Hence the missing volume
in the cone over a measurable \(E\subseteq F\) is
\[
\frac{h_F}{d}\int_E w_F\,d\sigma_F
=\frac{|S|}{d+1}\int_E w_F\,d\mu_F,
\tag{10}
\]
where \(\mu_F\) is normalized facet probability. The last equality
uses that the cones from the centroid to all \(d+1\) facets
have volume \(|S|/(d+1)\).
The cones partition \(S\) up to volume-null interfaces.

Applying (2) to \(f_F\), followed by (9), gives the weighted
radial-strip estimate
\[
\int_{\{|s_i-b|\le\eta\}}w_F\,d\mu_F
\le \frac{C_{d-1,b}\eta}{(1-\delta)^d}
\int_F w_F\,d\mu_F,\qquad
0\le\eta\le r_{d-1,b}.
\tag{11}
\]
This is uniform even if the missing mass on a facet is
arbitrarily small or concentrated near its boundary.

## 3. Near-canonical cap losses

Let \(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d\) be the barycentric coordinates
of \(S\), put \(b=1/(d+1)\), and fix a canonical through-centroid
cap
\[
H_i^0=\{x:\lambda_i(x)-b\ge0\}.
\]
Let \(H=\{x:a(x)\ge0\}\) be another closed affine halfspace,
normalized so that
\[
\sup_{x\in S}|a(x)-(\lambda_i(x)-b)|\le\eta.
\tag{12}
\]
This normalization is part of the hypothesis; multiplying a
halfspace margin by an arbitrary positive number without
tracking (12) would not measure closeness.

If
\[
0\le\eta\le\frac{1-\delta}{4(d+1)},
\tag{13}
\]
then
\[
|(S\setminus K)\cap(H\mathbin{\triangle}H_i^0)|
\le \frac{8(d+1)}{(1-\delta)^{d+1}}\,
\eta\,|S\setminus K|.
\tag{14}
\]
In particular, defining the actual missing-cap loss by
\[
L_K(H)=|S\cap H|-|K\cap H|=|(S\setminus K)\cap H|,
\]
one obtains
\[
|L_K(H)-L_K(H_i^0)|
\le \frac{8(d+1)}{(1-\delta)^{d+1}}\,
\eta\,|S\setminus K|.
\tag{15}
\]

To prove this, any disagreement point \(x\in S\) obeys
\(|\lambda_i(x)-b|\le\eta\). At a missing point on the facet
ray \(x=g+a(p-g)\), one has \(a\ge1-\delta\) and the EXACT
identity
\[
\lambda_i(x)-b=a(\lambda_i(p)-b).
\tag{16}
\]
Thus its boundary direction lies in the facet strip
\[
|\lambda_i(p)-b|\le\eta/(1-\delta).
\tag{17}
\]
There is no additional \(O(\delta)\) location error: the
reference plane passes through \(g\).

On the opposite facet \(\{\lambda_i=0\}\), (17) is impossible
under (13), since the constant distance is \(b\). On every
other facet, \(\lambda_i\) is a facet barycentric coordinate,
so (11) applies. Here
\[
r_{d-1,\,1/(d+1)}=\frac1{4(d+1)},\qquad
C_{d-1,\,1/(d+1)}=8(d+1).
\]
Apply (11) with width \(\eta/(1-\delta)\), use (10), and
sum the missing volumes of those facet cones. Their sum is
at most the total missing volume, so no further factor of
the number of facets is needed. This proves (14)-(15).

All boundaries and cone interfaces have zero \(d\)-volume;
closed-cap conventions introduce no extra term. If
\(K=S\), both sides are zero. The assertion is uniform in
the shape of \(K\), subject only to (6).

For example, when \(\delta\le1/[2(d+1)]\), Bernoulli gives
\((1-\delta)^{d+1}\ge1/2\). The right side of (15) is then
at most \(16(d+1)\eta\,|S\setminus K|\).

## 4. Normal and meeting-point perturbations; scope

The affine-margin condition covers simultaneous small normal
and point motions. Write
\[
\lambda_i(x)-b=l_i\cdot(x-g),\qquad
u_i=l_i/|l_i|.
\]
For a unit normal \(u\) and a point \(y\), take
\(a(x)=|l_i|\,u\cdot(x-y)\). If
\(R_S=\max_{x\in S}|x-g|\), then
\[
\sup_S|a-(\lambda_i-b)|
\le |l_i|\big(R_S|u-u_i|+|y-g|\big).
\tag{18}
\]
Thus the right side of (18) can be used as \(\eta\) in (15).
Alternatively (12) is an affine-invariant way of specifying the
perturbation, with no conditioning assumption on the simplex.

The estimate holds separately and uniformly for every canonical
index. If losses from several caps are summed, their individual
bounds may be summed; a union or multiplicity comparison then
carries the corresponding sum of perturbation sizes.

This controls near-canonical missing-cap errors relative to the
actual missing mass. It does not itself prove a relation between
maximum-depth deficit and missing mass, nor control directions
outside the stated cap neighborhoods. No global stability or
mixed-integer extraction statement is assumed.

The companion verifier
../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_convex_facet_strip_missing_cap_loss.py passes 6264 exact
convex-ridge strip integrals, 1045 radial-weight comparisons, and
72 actual planar missing-cap comparisons. The last examples retain
all facet centroids and include missing masses tending to zero
through arbitrarily thin boundary triangles. The proof above
establishes the uniform assertion beyond these finite checks.
